newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korea's Hanbo graft probe winds down.
newsitem.headline: S.Korea's Hanbo graft probe winds down.

text.p: With a clutch of President Kim Young-sam's closest political allies and top bankers in custody, South Korean prosecutors on Friday said a probe into a loans-for-kickbacks scandal was now winding down.
But opposition parties and newspapers claimed a cover-up and said the prosecution had failed to ferret out the top people behind the crisis involving loans to the failed Hanbo Steel Co.
A prosecution official said no further summonses were expected on Friday as the three-week investigation approached its final phase.
"We have no plans to summons anybody today," he said by telephone. "We don't want to rule out the possibility of more summonses in coming days but it wouldn't be anyone heavyweight."

Prosecutors were now focusing on unearthing evidence to support charges against nine people arrested for their roles in a scandal in which a firm with a net worth of just $300 million wrung $5.8 billion from a pliant financial system.

Those held include a former cabinet minister and three lawmakers from the ruling party -- among them Kim's top loyalists -- one opposition legislator, two bankers plus the founder of Hanbo Group and his former financial officer.
Hanbo Steel, flagship of South Korea's 14th largest conglomerate, was declared insolvent on January 23.

The scandal has tarnished Kim's "Mr Clean" image and confused the issue of who will succeed him as president. Kim cannot seek a second term in elections in December and his role as kingmaker is now in jeopardy, throwing the contest wide open.
Senior prosecutor Choi Byung-koog told reporters on Thursday there would be "no more politicians or government officials called in for questioning".
Kim Woo-suk resigned as Home Affairs minister on Wednesday and was taken into custody the next day on charges of taking bribes from Hanbo in return for favours.

Detained with the minister were ruling New Korea Party stalwart Hwang Byung-tai, who helped engineer the president's rise to power, and Kwon Roh-kap, a top aide to opposition leader Kim Dae-jung. Both politicians were charged with bribery.
But opposition parties and newspapers claimed the prosecution had only touched the tip of the iceburg.
"Prosecutors are putting on the biggest show ever," the main opposition National Congress for New Politics said in a statement on Friday.

"Bringing an end to the Hanbo investigation is like tricking the public in broad daylight," it said. "Prosecutors are covering up and manipulating the probe. It has only touched the little branches, not the root or the stem."
The party demanded another all-out investigation focusing on government officials and those close to Kim Young-sam.
An editorial in the Hankook Ilbo newspaper said questions over how Hanbo was able to borrow so much money and where the missing millions had gone had yet to be answered.
"The public demands a thorough investigation that offers no sanctuary," it said.
